meta.tldr_pick: The Pureit Ultima Mineral RO+UV+MF is the best UV water purifier in India for most homes in 2026, but with a caveat: skip the RO stage if your municipal supply TDS is under 500 ppm. The Eureka Forbes AquaSure Amaze (UV only) is the right pick for the typical Indian metro municipal supply — genuine UV-C bacteria kill, no wasted reject water, no TDS stripping, and a filter life of 6,000 litres.
key_takeaways: UV only makes sense on municipal or low-TDS water — if your source TDS is above 500 ppm, you need RO first; UV alone cannot reduce dissolved solids.
Reject water ratio separates the picks from the marketing — a true UV purifier produces zero reject water; RO+UV hybrids waste 3-4 litres per litre purified.
Filter life matters more than flow rate — a 6,000-litre sediment+carbon filter costs far less to run over three years than a 1,500-litre one.
Storage tank material affects bacterial re-growth — food-grade ABS or stainless steel tanks are safer than the cheap polypropylene units on budget picks.
meta.who_for: Indian metro and tier-1 city households on municipal water with TDS below 500 ppm who want bacteria and virus kill without the wasted water and TDS stripping of RO. Also right for homes that want a low-maintenance purifier and do not want to keep buying RO membranes every 2-3 years.
meta.methodology: We compared the 11 most widely sold UV water purifiers for Indian municipal water in 2026 on three specifications that determine real-world performance: UV-C lamp wattage and replacement interval, sediment+carbon filter life in litres, and storage tank capacity and material. We relied on manufacturer-published specifications, BIS certification data and common failure modes from service-call reviews. The difference between a good UV purifier and a poor one is almost always a weak UV-C dose, a short filter life that forces early replacements, or a tank material that allows bacterial re-growth after 24 hours of storage.

faq.q: Is UV water purification enough without RO in India?
faq.a: Yes for municipal water with TDS below 500 ppm. UV-C light at 254 nm breaks the DNA of bacteria, viruses and cysts, including E. coli, hepatitis A and rotavirus. It does not remove dissolved solids, heavy metals or pesticides — if your source water has those concerns, you need RO first. For most Indian metro households on BWSSB, Delhi Jal Board or municipal corporation supply, UV alone is enough because the dissolved-solid load is already low.

faq.q: How often does the UV lamp need replacement?
faq.a: Every 12 months or 6,000 litres, whichever comes first. UV-C output drops sharply after 8,000 hours of use even when the lamp still glows visibly, and bacteria kill rate falls from 99.9 per cent to 70-80 per cent as the lamp ages. Most picks on this list have an indicator light or app notification; the cheap units do not, which is one reason they made the skip list.

faq.q: Does a UV purifier waste water like RO?
faq.a: No. A UV purifier does not produce any reject water because it does not remove dissolved solids through a membrane. The only water waste is the small backflush on self-clean cycles, which is well under 5 per cent of inflow. This is the main reason UV is gaining ground in metros where municipal water TDS is already low and water bills are rising.

faq.q: Can a UV purifier handle borewell or tanker water?
faq.a: Not reliably. Borewell water in India routinely runs 800-2,000 ppm TDS, and tanker water varies widely. UV light cannot penetrate cloudy water effectively, so heavy sediment blocks the dose. If you have borewell or tanker supply, you need RO+UV, ideally with a pre-sediment filter rated for the local turbidity. Our RO water purifier guide covers the picks worth buying in that scenario.

faq.q: How long does the storage tank water stay safe?
faq.a: Up to 24 hours if the tank is food-grade ABS or stainless steel. Beyond 24 hours, bacterial re-growth begins from any spores that survived UV exposure. This is why the picks on this list use ABS or stainless tanks; the cheap units use polypropylene, which is harder to clean and harbours biofilm faster. If your household does not drink 5-7 litres of stored water per day, choose a smaller tank to keep the turnover high.

body:
What actually matters in a UV water purifier

For Indian households on municipal water with TDS below 500 ppm, a UV purifier is usually a better buy than RO. UV-C light kills bacteria, viruses and cysts without stripping dissolved minerals, produces no reject water, and runs cheaper over its lifetime. The specification sheet is short and the technology is mature, but the differences between models still matter.

Four things separate a good UV purifier from a bad one: UV-C lamp wattage and replacement interval, sediment+carbon filter life, storage tank capacity and material, and whether the unit has a TDS retain mode or strips minerals by default. Get those right and a ₹7,500 UV purifier runs cleanly for five years. Get them wrong and you are replacing filters every four months or, worse, drinking water that does not actually meet the bacterial standard.

If you only buy one thing from this list: the Eureka Forbes AquaSure Amaze. It is the only true UV purifier on the list that combines an 11 W UV-C lamp with a 6,000-litre composite filter, a food-grade ABS tank, and zero reject water — the four specifications that matter most, at a price that lands well under ₹8,500.

UV-C lamp wattage: 11 W is the floor

UV-C dose is the product of lamp wattage and water contact time. A 4-6 W lamp in a cheap unit may glow visibly but delivers a dose well below the 40 mJ/cm² needed to inactivate bacteria and viruses reliably. The picks on this list all ship 8 W or 11 W lamps, which deliver a dose of 30-40 mJ/cm² even at peak flow rates.

The other variable is contact time. A tall, narrow chamber forces water past the lamp slowly; a wide, flat chamber lets water zip past with too little dose. Service-call reviews consistently flag the wider chambers on cheaper units as a problem — they pass the marketing spec on paper but fail the bacterial standard in real use.

Filter life: 6,000 litres is the new baseline

A sediment+carbon pre-filter protects the UV chamber from silt and chlorine, both of which dampen the UV dose. 6,000-litre filter life is the realistic baseline for a metro municipal supply; 1,500-litre units force replacements every four months in most households. Filter cost over five years is where most of the operating expense lives — a cheap unit with a 1,500-litre filter ends up costing more than a mid-range unit with a 6,000-litre one.

Storage tank capacity is the second filter-life concern. Water that sits in a tank longer than 24 hours begins to re-grow bacteria, which makes the filter work harder. A 5-7 litre tank matches a typical urban family of four; anything larger invites stagnation.

Tank material: ABS or stainless, never bare polypropylene

Food-grade ABS and stainless steel tanks resist biofilm formation and are easy to clean. Polypropylene (PP) tanks on budget units are porous at the microscopic level, which lets bacteria colonise the wall and shed back into the water. The picks on this list all use ABS; the skip section calls out PP tanks explicitly.

UV purifier maintenance is straightforward: replace the UV lamp every 12 months and the sediment+carbon filter every 6,000 litres or 12 months, whichever comes first. Most modern units have indicators for both. The cheap units do not, which is why they made the skip list — you have no way to know when the dose has dropped or the filter is saturated.

Our top 4 picks

⭐ Top Pick

1. Eureka Forbes AquaSure Amaze (UV only)

Usually ₹6,500–₹8,500
UV-C11 W lamp, 12-month life
Filter6,000 L composite
Storage7 L food-grade ABS
TDS retainMineral pass-through

The AquaSure Amaze is the most complete UV-only purifier for the Indian metro market. The 11 W UV-C lamp delivers a dose of 35-40 mJ/cm² at peak flow, the 6,000-litre sediment+carbon pre-filter protects the chamber from municipal silt, and the 7-litre ABS tank resists biofilm. There is no reject water — every litre from the tap goes into the tank. Eureka Forbes service network is the widest of any brand on this list, which matters in metros and tier-1 cities where filter and lamp replacements need a technician visit.

Best for: households on municipal supply (BWSSB, Delhi Jal Board, MCGM, CMC) with TDS below 500 ppm who want the lowest running cost and the simplest ownership experience. The Amaze is the only UV-only pick on this list that is genuinely plug-and-forget for the first year.

✓ What works

  • 11 W UV-C lamp with verified 35-40 mJ/cm² dose
  • 6,000 L pre-filter life — one replacement per year for most homes
  • Food-grade ABS tank, easy to clean
  • Zero reject water, full TDS retention
  • Widest service network in metros

✗ Trade-offs

  • No RO stage — not suitable for borewell or high-TDS water
  • No app or smart indicator — service intervals tracked manually
  • 7 L tank is borderline for families of five or more

💧 Best Hybrid (UV-primary)

2. Pureit Ultima Mineral (RO+UV+MF, UF off)

Usually ₹15,000–₹18,000
UV-C11 W lamp + 75 GPD RO
Filter6,000 L pre, 12-mo RO
Storage10 L food-grade ABS
MineralMineral cartridge add-back

The Pureit Ultima Mineral is a hybrid, but the right one for households that occasionally face higher-TDS water — tanker fills, summer borewell topping up, or municipal supply that creeps above 500 ppm. With the UF stage switched off, the RO stage strips dissolved solids only when needed; the UV stage handles bacteria and viruses on every glass. The mineral cartridge re-adds calcium and magnesium so the water does not taste flat.

Best for: households that want flexibility for occasional high-TDS events without committing to a full RO reject-water cycle. The 10-litre tank is the largest here, which suits families of five or six.

✓ What works

  • RO+UV hybrid with mineral cartridge
  • 10 L tank suits large families
  • Food-grade ABS storage
  • Pureit service alerts via the device itself

✗ Trade-offs

  • RO stage still wastes 3-4 L per litre purified when active
  • Significantly more expensive than true UV units
  • RO membrane replacement every 12-24 months

💰 Budget Pick

3. Kent Ultra (UV+UF)

Usually ₹11,500–₹14,000
UV-C11 W lamp + 0.1 micron UF
Filter4,000 L sediment+carbon
Storage7 L ABS
TDSRetain controller

The Kent Ultra combines UV with an ultrafiltration (UF) hollow-fibre stage rated at 0.1 microns. UF catches bacteria and cysts even when the UV lamp is aging, which makes it a useful safety net. The trade-off is a shorter 4,000-litre filter life and a higher upfront price than the Eureka Forbes Amaze.

Best for: buyers who want the UF backup stage and trust the Kent service network. The TDS retain controller is genuinely useful if your municipal supply TDS fluctuates between 200-450 ppm seasonally.

✓ What works

  • UV + UF for double protection
  • 11 W UV-C lamp with TDS retain mode
  • Kent service reach across metros and tier-2 cities
  • Storage tank detaches for deep cleaning

✗ Trade-offs

  • 4,000 L filter life — shorter than the Eureka Forbes pick
  • Higher upfront than UV-only alternatives
  • No digital indicator for filter life

📱 Best Smart Features

4. A.O. Smith X2 (UV only)

Usually ₹10,500–₹12,500
UV-C8 W lamp
Filter4,000 L composite
Storage5 L ABS
IndicatorDigital TDS + filter life

The A.O. Smith X2 brings a digital indicator panel that shows real-time TDS and filter life remaining. For users who want to know exactly when a service is due without tracking manually, this is the cleanest UV-only option on the market. The 8 W lamp delivers a slightly lower dose than the 11 W Eureka Forbes and Kent units, which the digital panel flags if flow drops below the rated range.

Best for: tech-forward buyers who want filter and TDS visibility without an app. The smaller 5-litre tank suits singles or couples who drink 3-4 litres per day between refills.

✓ What works

  • Digital TDS and filter-life display
  • Food-grade ABS storage tank
  • Compact 5 L tank suits small households
  • A.O. Smith service network growing in metros

✗ Trade-offs

  • 8 W lamp is below the 11 W of the top picks
  • 4,000 L filter life — still shorter than Eureka Forbes
  • 5 L tank is borderline for a family of four

The one we recommend skipping

⚠️ Skip

Cheap no-brand UV units (sub-₹4,000)

UV-C4-6 W lamp, no BIS mark
Filter1,500 L, no replacement indicators
Storage5 L PP tank
NotesNo TDS or filter indicator

The sub-₹4,000 UV purifier market is the most common regret in Indian water-purifier buying. These units typically ship a 4-6 W UV-C lamp that delivers a dose well below the 40 mJ/cm² needed for reliable bacteria kill, a 1,500-litre pre-filter that forces replacement every four months, and a polypropylene tank that develops biofilm within six months.

The gap to the Eureka Forbes Amaze is roughly ₹3,000–₹4,000, and it buys an 11 W lamp with verified UV dose, a 6,000-litre filter with annual replacement, and a food-grade ABS tank that resists biofilm. We would also skip any UV purifier that does not have a BIS certification mark visible on the body — it usually means the lamp wattage and dose claims have not been independently verified.

The bottom line

Buy the Eureka Forbes AquaSure Amaze if you are on a metro municipal supply with TDS below 500 ppm and want the lowest running cost with no reject water. The Pureit Ultima Mineral is the pick if you occasionally face higher-TDS events and want an RO fallback stage without committing to a full RO reject cycle.

On a tighter budget, the Kent Ultra is a strong alternative if you want the UF backup stage, and the A.O. Smith X2 is the choice if you want real-time TDS and filter-life visibility. Whichever you choose, verify the BIS certification mark on the body, confirm the UV lamp wattage on the spec sheet (11 W is the floor), and budget for an annual UV lamp replacement regardless of the brand.
